--- title: "Free Fall Beyond Idealization: Air Resistance, Terminal Velocity, and Real-World Dissipative Corrections" subtitle: "A progressive escalation from vacuum ballistic motion to linear drag, quadratic turbulence, buoyancy, barometric density decay, and Coriolis deflection." description: "A comprehensive applied mechanics treatise expanding textbook free fall into real-world reality: Archimedes buoyancy, Stokes linear drag, Rayleigh quadratic turbulence, hyperbolic velocity solutions, stratosphere density decay, altitude-dependent gravity, and the Coriolis eastward deflection." author: "Igor Kan" date: "2026-10-29" categories: [Preprints, Physics, Classical Mechanics, Kinematics, Dynamics, Fluid Dynamics] draft: false format: html: toc: true toc-depth: 3 --- ::: {.callout-note} ### Preprint / Working Draft This article is published under the **Preprints** category. It represents an active paper investigating the progressive hierarchy of non-ideal dissipative, aerodynamic, and planetary corrections to gravitational free fall. ::: --- ## 1. Introduction: The Collapse of the Galilean Vacuum In introductory physics, the motion of falling bodies is almost universally modeled through Galileo's famous vacuum idealization: $$m \frac{d^2 y}{dt^2} = -m g \implies \ddot{y} = -g \tag{1}$$ Equation (1) asserts that all objects—regardless of mass, shape, or density—accelerate downward at the exact same constant rate $g \approx 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$. In 1971, Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott demonstrated this principle dramatically on the airless surface of the Moon, dropping a $1.32\text{ kg}$ geological hammer and a $0.03\text{ kg}$ falcon feather simultaneously; both struck the lunar regolith in unison. However, inside a planetary atmosphere, **the Galilean idealization collapses**. A skydiver in Earth's troposphere does not accelerate indefinitely; a falling mist droplet does not crash at hundreds of kilometers per hour; and a stone dropped from a high tower does not strike the earth directly below its plumb line. The real physical world introduces a hierarchy of dissipative forces, thermodynamic couplings, and rotating-frame inertial effects: ```{mermaid} flowchart TD G["0. Galilean Baseline (Ideal Vacuum)
m a = -m g"] --> B["1. Archimedes Buoyancy
m a = -m g_eff"] B --> S["2. Stokes Linear Viscous Drag (Re ≪ 1)
m a = -m g_eff - b v"] B --> R["3. Rayleigh Quadratic Turbulent Drag (Re ≫ 10³)
m a = -m g_eff + ½ ρ C_d A v²"] R --> H["4. Stratospheric Vertical Gradients
Variable ρ(z) & g(z)"] H --> C["5. Rotating Planetary Non-Inertial Frame
Coriolis Deflection -2m (Ω × v)"] ``` --- ## 2. Correction 1: Hydrodynamic Buoyancy (Archimedes' Principle) Whenever a solid body of mass $m$, volume $V$, and average density $\rho_b = m/V$ is submerged in a fluid of ambient density $\rho_f$, the fluid exerts an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the displaced fluid: $$F_{\text{buoyancy}} = +\rho_f V g \hat{\mathbf{j}} \tag{2}$$ ```{mermaid} flowchart TD subgraph Body["Hydrodynamic Free-Body Equilibrium"] direction TB F_b["▲ Upward Buoyant Force: F_buoyancy = ρ_fluid · V · g"] CG["● Center of Mass (m, V)"] W["▼ Downward Gravitational Weight: W = m · g"] end ``` Writing the net static gravitational force: $$F_{\text{net}} = -m g + \rho_f V g = -m g \left( 1 - \frac{\rho_f V}{m} \right) = -m g \left( 1 - \frac{\rho_f}{\rho_b} \right) \tag{3}$$ We define the **effective gravitational acceleration** $g_{\text{eff}}$: $$g_{\text{eff}} = g \left( 1 - \frac{\rho_f}{\rho_b} \right) \tag{4}$$ ### When Does Buoyancy Matter? | Physical System | Body Density $\rho_b$ | Fluid Density $\rho_f$ | Effective Gravity $g_{\text{eff}}$ | Buoyancy Correction Magnitude | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Steel sphere in air** | $7{,}800\text{ kg/m}^3$ | $1.2\text{ kg/m}^3$ | $0.99985 \, g$ | $0.015\%$ (Completely negligible) | | **Styrofoam bead in air** | $15\text{ kg/m}^3$ | $1.2\text{ kg/m}^3$ | $0.92000 \, g$ | $8.0\%$ (Moderate engineering impact) | | **Sand grain in water** | $2{,}600\text{ kg/m}^3$ | $1{,}000\text{ kg/m}^3$ | $0.61538 \, g$ | $38.5\%$ (Dominant control of settling) | | **Helium balloon in air** | $0.18\text{ kg/m}^3$ | $1.2\text{ kg/m}^3$ | $-5.6667 \, g$ | Upward acceleration (Aerostat flight) | --- ## 3. Correction 2: Linear Viscous Drag (The Stokes Regime, $\mathrm{Re} \ll 1$) When a body moves through a fluid at very low speeds, or when the body's characteristic dimension is microscopic, fluid inertia is negligible compared to fluid viscous shear. This is characterized by a low **Reynolds number**: $$\mathrm{Re} = \frac{\rho_f v D}{\mu} \ll 1 \tag{5}$$ Under this creeping flow regime, the resistive drag force is strictly **linear in velocity**: $$F_{\text{drag}} = -b v \tag{6}$$ For a smooth sphere of diameter $D$ in a fluid with dynamic viscosity $\mu$, George Gabriel Stokes famously derived the drag constant: $$b = 3 \pi \mu D \tag{7}$$ ### Analytical Solution of the Linear Free-Fall ODE Taking downward as negative and letting $v(t) = \dot{y}(t) \le 0$: $$m \frac{dv}{dt} = -m g_{\text{eff}} - b v \iff \frac{dv}{dt} + \frac{b}{m} v = -g_{\text{eff}} \tag{8}$$ We define two fundamental physical parameters: $$\tau = \frac{m}{b} \quad (\text{Characteristic Velocity Relaxation Time}), \qquad v_t = \frac{m g_{\text{eff}}}{b} = g_{\text{eff}} \tau \quad (\text{Terminal Speed}) \tag{9}$$ Equation (8) is a first-order linear ordinary differential equation. Multiplying by the integrating factor $e^{t/\tau}$: $$\frac{d}{dt} \left( v(t) e^{t/\tau} \right) = -g_{\text{eff}} e^{t/\tau}$$ Integrating from initial velocity $v(0) = v_0$: $$v(t) e^{t/\tau} - v_0 = -g_{\text{eff}} \tau \left( e^{t/\tau} - 1 \right) = -v_t \left( e^{t/\tau} - 1 \right)$$ $$v(t) = -v_t + \left( v_0 + v_t \right) e^{-t/\tau} \tag{10}$$ For a body dropped from rest ($v_0 = 0$): $$v(t) = -v_t \left( 1 - e^{-t/\tau} \right) \tag{11}$$ ### Position Trajectory via Integration Integrating velocity $v(t) = \frac{dy}{dt}$ from initial altitude $y(0) = y_0$: $$y(t) = y_0 - \int_0^t v_t \left( 1 - e^{-t'/\tau} \right) dt' = y_0 - v_t t + v_t \int_0^t e^{-t'/\tau} dt'$$ $$y(t) = y_0 - v_t t + v_t \tau \left( 1 - e^{-t/\tau} \right) \tag{12}$$ ### Asymptotic Limiting Analysis Let us subject Equation (12) to the extreme-case torture test: 1. **Short-Time Asymptote ($t \ll \tau$):** Taylor expanding the exponential $e^{-t/\tau} = 1 - \frac{t}{\tau} + \frac{t^2}{2\tau^2} - \frac{t^3}{6\tau^3} + \dots$: $$y(t) = y_0 - v_t t + v_t \tau \left[ \frac{t}{\tau} - \frac{t^2}{2\tau^2} + \frac{t^3}{6\tau^3} \right] = y_0 - v_t t + v_t t - \frac{v_t}{2\tau} t^2 + \mathcal{O}(t^3)$$ Recalling that $v_t / \tau = g_{\text{eff}}$: $$y(t) \approx y_0 - \frac{1}{2} g_{\text{eff}} t^2 \tag{13}$$ **Result:** In the limit of early times, linear air resistance is completely negligible, and the solution collapses *identically* into Galileo's vacuum parabola! 2. **Long-Time Asymptote ($t \gg \tau$):** The exponential term decays to zero ($e^{-t/\tau} \to 0$): $$y(t) \to (y_0 + v_t \tau) - v_t t \tag{14}$$ The trajectory becomes a pure straight line of constant terminal velocity $-v_t$. Acceleration has vanished completely. --- ## 4. Correction 3: Quadratic Turbulent Drag (The Rayleigh Regime, $\mathrm{Re} \gg 10^3$) For macroscopic objects falling in air—such as raindrops larger than $1\text{ mm}$, baseballs, vehicles, and skydivers—the Reynolds number is high ($\mathrm{Re} = 10^4 \text{ to } 10^7$). In this regime, viscous skin friction is eclipsed by **form drag** caused by turbulent flow separation and wake pressure deficits. Lord Rayleigh formulated the drag force as proportional to velocity squared: $$F_{\text{drag}} = -\frac{1}{2} \rho_f C_d A v |v| \tag{15}$$ Where $C_d$ is the dimensionless drag coefficient, $A$ is the projected cross-sectional area, and $|v|$ ensures drag always opposes the instantaneous direction of motion. ### Downward Motion from Rest For downward motion ($v \le 0$), the drag acts upward ($+v^2$): $$m \frac{dv}{dt} = -m g_{\text{eff}} + \frac{1}{2} \rho_f C_d A v^2 \tag{16}$$ At terminal velocity $v_t$, acceleration ceases ($\frac{dv}{dt} = 0$): $$m g_{\text{eff}} = \frac{1}{2} \rho_f C_d A v_t^2 \implies v_t = \sqrt{\frac{2 m g_{\text{eff}}}{\rho_f C_d A}} \tag{17}$$ Rewriting Equation (16) using $v_t$: $$\frac{dv}{dt} = -g_{\text{eff}} \left( 1 - \frac{v^2}{v_t^2} \right) \tag{18}$$ ### Exact Analytical Solution via Separation of Variables $$\int_0^{v(t)} \frac{dv'}{1 - \left(\frac{v'}{v_t}\right)^2} = -g_{\text{eff}} \int_0^t dt'$$ Recall the standard integral $\int \frac{dx}{1 - x^2} = \operatorname{arctanh}(x)$ for $|x| < 1$: $$v_t \operatorname{arctanh}\left( \frac{v(t)}{v_t} \right) = -g_{\text{eff}} t \implies \frac{v(t)}{v_t} = \tanh\left( -\frac{g_{\text{eff}} t}{v_t} \right)$$ Because $\tanh(-x) = -\tanh(x)$: $$v(t) = -v_t \tanh\left( \frac{g_{\text{eff}} t}{v_t} \right) \tag{19}$$ ### Exact Closed-Form Position Trajectory Integrating Equation (19) using $\int \tanh(u)\,du = \ln(\cosh u)$: $$y(t) = y_0 - v_t \int_0^t \tanh\left( \frac{g_{\text{eff}} t'}{v_t} \right) dt' = y_0 - \frac{v_t^2}{g_{\text{eff}}} \ln\left[ \cosh\left( \frac{g_{\text{eff}} t}{v_t} \right) \right] \tag{20}$$ ::: {#cell-fig-drag-comparison .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show Python generation code"} import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt # Physical constants g = 9.81 vt = 50.0 # Matched terminal speed in m/s (~180 km/h for skydiver) tau = vt / g # Relaxation time (~5.1 s) y0 = 500.0 # Drop height in meters # Time grid t = np.linspace(0, 15.0, 400) # 1. Galilean Vacuum v_vac = -g * t y_vac = y0 - 0.5 * g * t**2 # 2. Linear Stokes Drag v_lin = -vt * (1.0 - np.exp(-t / tau)) y_lin = y0 - vt * t + vt * tau * (1.0 - np.exp(-t / tau)) # 3. Quadratic Rayleigh Drag v_quad = -vt * np.tanh(g * t / vt) y_quad = y0 - (vt**2 / g) * np.log(np.cosh(g * t / vt)) # Plotting fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5), dpi=150) # Panel 1: Velocity ax1.plot(t, v_vac, ':', color='gray', linewidth=2, label='Galilean Vacuum: $v = -gt$') ax1.plot(t, v_lin, '--', color='#d9534f', linewidth=2.5, label='Linear Stokes: $v = -v_t(1 - e^{-t/\\tau})$') ax1.plot(t, v_quad, '-', color='#0275d8', linewidth=2.5, label='Quadratic Rayleigh: $v = -v_t\\tanh(gt/v_t)$') ax1.axhline(-vt, color='black', linestyle='-.', linewidth=1, label=f'Terminal Velocity $v_t = -{vt:.0f}$ m/s') ax1.set_title('Velocity Evolution: Drag Regimes vs. Vacuum', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold', pad=10) ax1.set_xlabel('Elapsed Time $t$ (seconds)', fontsize=11) ax1.set_ylabel('Velocity $v(t)$ (m/s)', fontsize=11) ax1.set_ylim(-90, 5) ax1.legend(loc='lower left', frameon=True, fontsize=9) ax1.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.6) # Panel 2: Altitude ax2.plot(t, y_vac, ':', color='gray', linewidth=2, label='Galilean Vacuum') ax2.plot(t, y_lin, '--', color='#d9534f', linewidth=2.5, label='Linear Stokes Drag') ax2.plot(t, y_quad, '-', color='#0275d8', linewidth=2.5, label='Quadratic Rayleigh Drag') ax2.axhline(0, color='black', linestyle='-', linewidth=1) ax2.set_title('Altitude Trajectory $y(t)$', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold', pad=10) ax2.set_xlabel('Elapsed Time $t$ (seconds)', fontsize=11) ax2.set_ylabel('Altitude $y(t)$ (meters)', fontsize=11) ax2.set_ylim(-20, 520) ax2.legend(loc='upper right', frameon=True, fontsize=9) ax2.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.6) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Comparison of Free-Fall Velocity v(t) and Altitude y(t) across three fundamental physical models: Ideal Galilean Vacuum (no drag), Stokes Linear Drag (exponential relaxation), and Rayleigh Quadratic Drag (hyperbolic tangent saturation).](index_files/figure-html/fig-drag-comparison-output-1.png){#fig-drag-comparison width=1932 height=732} ::: ::: --- ### The Upward-Flight Asymmetry: Breaking Time-Reversal Symmetry In vacuum kinematics, ascending and descending paths are strictly symmetric: $t_{\text{ascent}} = t_{\text{descent}}$. Under quadratic drag, **this symmetry is completely shattered**. During upward ascent ($v > 0$), gravity and drag act in the *same* downward direction: $$m \frac{dv}{dt} = -m g_{\text{eff}} - \frac{1}{2} \rho C_d A v^2 = -g_{\text{eff}} \left( 1 + \frac{v^2}{v_t^2} \right) \tag{21}$$ Separating variables using $\int \frac{dx}{1 + x^2} = \arctan(x)$: $$\int_{v_0}^{v(t)} \frac{dv'}{1 + (v'/v_t)^2} = -g_{\text{eff}} t \implies \arctan\left(\frac{v}{v_t}\right) - \arctan\left(\frac{v_0}{v_t}\right) = -\frac{g_{\text{eff}} t}{v_t}$$ $$v(t) = v_t \tan\left[ \arctan\left(\frac{v_0}{v_t}\right) - \frac{g_{\text{eff}} t}{v_t} \right] \tag{22}$$ Setting $v(t_{\text{apex}}) = 0$ yields the ascent time: $$t_{\text{ascent}} = \frac{v_t}{g_{\text{eff}}} \arctan\left( \frac{v_0}{v_t} \right) \tag{23}$$ Compare this to the descent time required to fall back from that exact same apex altitude $H$ to the ground under Equation (20): $$t_{\text{descent}} = \frac{v_t}{g_{\text{eff}}} \operatorname{arccosh}\left( \exp\left( \frac{g_{\text{eff}} H}{v_t^2} \right) \right) \tag{24}$$ Because energy was irreversibly dissipated into heat during ascent, the projectile reaches a lower peak height, and $t_{\text{ascent}} < t_{\text{descent}}$. Dissipation breaks the time-reversal invariance ($T$-symmetry) of the governing equations. --- ## 5. Correction 4: Stratospheric Drops (Barometric Density Decay and Altitude-Dependent Gravity) On October 14, 2012, Austrian skydiver Felix Baumgartner stepped out of a helium capsule at an altitude of $z_0 = 38{,}969\text{ m}$ ($127{,}851\text{ ft}$). During his free fall, he reached a maximum speed of $v_{\text{max}} = 1{,}357.6\text{ km/h}$ (Mach $1.25$), becoming the first human to break the sound barrier without vehicular propulsion. Why did Baumgartner reach Mach $1.25$ and subsequently **decelerate** before deploying his parachute? ### The Two Coupled Vertical Gradients 1. **Barometric Density Decay:** In an isothermal atmosphere of scale height $H \approx 8{,}500\text{ m}$: $$\rho(z) = \rho_0 \exp\left( -\frac{z}{H} \right) \tag{25}$$ At $39\text{ km}$, air density is $\rho \approx 1.2 \times e^{-39000/8500} \approx 0.012\text{ kg/m}^3$—less than $1\%$ of sea-level density! 2. **Inverse-Square Gravitational Field:** By Newton's law of universal gravitation: $$g(z) = g_0 \left( \frac{R_E}{R_E + z} \right)^2 \approx g_0 \left( 1 - \frac{2z}{R_E} \right) \tag{26}$$ At $39\text{ km}$, $g \approx 9.81 \times (6371 / 6410)^2 \approx 9.69\text{ m/s}^2$ (a $1.2\%$ reduction). ### The Dynamic Terminal Velocity Because terminal velocity scales as $v_t(z) = \sqrt{\frac{2 m g(z)}{\rho(z) C_d A}}$, substituting Equation (25) yields: $$v_t(z) \propto \exp\left( \frac{z}{2H} \right) \tag{27}$$ At $39\text{ km}$, the local terminal velocity is roughly $\sqrt{100} = 10$ times higher than at sea level ($v_t \approx 500\text{ m/s} \approx 1800\text{ km/h}$). As Baumgartner plunged into the denser troposphere, $\rho(z)$ increased exponentially, compressing $v_t(z)$ down to $\sim 55\text{ m/s}$ ($200\text{ km/h}$). ::: {#cell-fig-stratosphere-jump .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show Python generation code"} import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp # Stratospheric physical parameters m = 118.0 # Skydiver + pressure suit mass (kg) Cd = 0.7 # Delta-position body drag coefficient A = 0.8 # Cross-sectional area (m^2) H_scale = 8500.0 # Atmospheric scale height (m) rho0 = 1.225 # Sea level air density (kg/m^3) R_earth = 6371000.0 # Earth radius in meters g0 = 9.80665 def atmosphere_dynamics(t, state): z, v = state # z: altitude (m), v: vertical velocity (m/s, negative downward) # Altitude-dependent density and gravity rho = rho0 * np.exp(-max(z, 0) / H_scale) g_z = g0 * (R_earth / (R_earth + max(z, 0)))**2 # Drag force (opposes velocity) f_drag = 0.5 * rho * Cd * A * v**2 * np.sign(-v) # Equations of motion: dz/dt = v, dv/dt = -g + f_drag/m dzdt = v dvdt = -g_z + f_drag / m return [dzdt, dvdt] # Integrate from 38,969 m drop until chute deployment at 2,500 m z_init = 38969.0 v_init = 0.0 sol = solve_ivp(atmosphere_dynamics, [0, 260], [z_init, v_init], max_step=0.2, t_eval=np.linspace(0, 260, 1000)) # Speed in km/h and Mach estimate (speed of sound ~ 300-340 m/s depending on temp) speed_kmh = np.abs(sol.y[1]) * 3.6 mach_est = np.abs(sol.y[1]) / 310.0 fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5), dpi=150) # Altitude plot ax1.plot(sol.t, sol.y[0] / 1000.0, '-', color='#0275d8', linewidth=2.5) ax1.axhline(z_init / 1000.0, linestyle='--', color='gray', label=f'Drop Altitude ({z_init/1000:.1f} km)') ax1.axhline(2.5, linestyle=':', color='#d9534f', label='Parachute Deploy (2.5 km)') ax1.set_title('Altitude vs. Time: Stratospheric Free Fall', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold', pad=10) ax1.set_xlabel('Elapsed Time (seconds)', fontsize=11) ax1.set_ylabel('Altitude $z$ (kilometers)', fontsize=11) ax1.legend(frameon=True, fontsize=9) ax1.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.6) # Velocity / Mach plot ax2.plot(sol.t, speed_kmh, '-', color='#d9534f', linewidth=2.5, label='Vertical Speed (km/h)') ax2.axhline(1235.0, color='black', linestyle='--', linewidth=1.2, label='Sound Barrier (Mach 1.0 ≈ 1235 km/h)') max_idx = np.argmax(speed_kmh) t_peak = sol.t[max_idx] v_peak = speed_kmh[max_idx] z_peak = sol.y[0][max_idx] / 1000.0 ax2.plot(t_peak, v_peak, 'o', color='purple', markersize=8) ax2.annotate(f'Peak: {v_peak:.0f} km/h (Mach {mach_est[max_idx]:.2f})\nAltitude: {z_peak:.1f} km', xy=(t_peak, v_peak), xytext=(t_peak + 20, v_peak - 150), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='purple', lw=1.5), fontsize=9, fontweight='bold', color='purple') ax2.set_title('Speed Profile: Natural Aerodynamic Deceleration', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold', pad=10) ax2.set_xlabel('Elapsed Time (seconds)', fontsize=11) ax2.set_ylabel('Downward Speed (km/h)', fontsize=11) ax2.legend(loc='lower right', frameon=True, fontsize=9) ax2.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.6) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Numerical Simulation of a Stratospheric Skydive (Baumgartner Profile from 39 km). Due to exponential barometric density decay, the skydiver breaks the sound barrier (Mach 1.25) in thin stratospheric air, then experiences natural aerodynamic deceleration as air density increases in the troposphere.](index_files/figure-html/fig-stratosphere-jump-output-1.png){#fig-stratosphere-jump width=1933 height=735} ::: ::: --- ## 6. Correction 5: The Coriolis Eastward Deflection on a Rotating Earth If a dense lead cannonball is dropped from the top of a tall tower in vacuum (or negligible drag), does it hit the ground at the exact point vertically below the release site? **No.** Because the Earth rotates from west to east with angular speed $\Omega \approx 7.2921 \times 10^{-5}\text{ rad/s}$, an observer attached to the rotating Earth resides in a **non-inertial reference frame**. ### The Non-Inertial Equation of Motion In a frame rotating with constant angular velocity vector $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$: $$\mathbf{a}_{\text{apparent}} = \mathbf{g}_{\text{eff}} - 2 \left( \boldsymbol{\Omega} \times \mathbf{v} \right) - \boldsymbol{\Omega} \times \left( \boldsymbol{\Omega} \times \mathbf{r} \right) \tag{28}$$ Where $-2(\boldsymbol{\Omega} \times \mathbf{v})$ is the **Coriolis acceleration**, and $-\boldsymbol{\Omega} \times (\boldsymbol{\Omega} \times \mathbf{r})$ is the centrifugal acceleration (which is already absorbed into the local plumb-line gravity vector $\mathbf{g}_{\text{eff}}$). ### Coordinate Setup at Latitude $\lambda$ Erect local topocentric coordinates: * $\hat{\mathbf{i}}$ points **East** * $\hat{\mathbf{j}}$ points **North** * $\hat{\mathbf{k}}$ points **Up** (local vertical) The Earth's angular velocity vector at latitude $\lambda$ is: $$\boldsymbol{\Omega} = 0 \, \hat{\mathbf{i}} + (\Omega \cos \lambda) \hat{\mathbf{j}} + (\Omega \sin \lambda) \hat{\mathbf{k}} \tag{29}$$ To leading order, the particle falls vertically downward with velocity: $$\mathbf{v}(t) \approx -g t \, \hat{\mathbf{k}} \tag{30}$$ ### Computing the Coriolis Cross Product $$\boldsymbol{\Omega} \times \mathbf{v} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{\mathbf{i}} & \hat{\mathbf{j}} & \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\ 0 & \Omega \cos \lambda & \Omega \sin \lambda \\ 0 & 0 & -g t \end{vmatrix} = \hat{\mathbf{i}} \left[ (\Omega \cos \lambda)(-g t) - 0 \right] = -\Omega g t \cos \lambda \, \hat{\mathbf{i}} \tag{31}$$ The Coriolis acceleration is: $$\mathbf{a}_{\text{coriolis}} = -2 \left( \boldsymbol{\Omega} \times \mathbf{v} \right) = -2 \left( -\Omega g t \cos \lambda \, \hat{\mathbf{i}} \right) = +2 \Omega g t \cos \lambda \, \hat{\mathbf{i}} \tag{32}$$ Notice the sign: $+2 \Omega g t \cos \lambda$ points strictly along $+\hat{\mathbf{i}}$—**toward the East**! ### Exact Closed-Form Eastward Deflection Integrating Equation (32) twice with initial conditions $x(0) = 0, \dot{x}(0) = 0$: $$\dot{x}(t) = \int_0^t 2 \Omega g t' \cos \lambda \, dt' = \Omega g t^2 \cos \lambda \tag{33}$$ $$x_{\text{east}}(t) = \int_0^t \Omega g (t')^2 \cos \lambda \, dt' = \frac{1}{3} \Omega g t^3 \cos \lambda \tag{34}$$ The total time to fall from height $h$ is $t_f = \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}$. Substituting $t_f$ into Equation (34): $$d_{\text{east}} = \frac{1}{3} \Omega g \cos \lambda \left( \frac{2h}{g} \right)^{3/2} = \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3} \Omega \cos \lambda \sqrt{\frac{h^3}{g}} \tag{35}$$ ::: {#cell-fig-coriolis-deflection .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show Python generation code"} import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt Omega = 7.292115e-5 # Earth rotation rate in rad/s g = 9.80665 # Height sweep from 10 m to 400 m h = np.linspace(10, 400, 300) # Latitudes: Equator (0 deg), 30 deg, 45 deg, 60 deg latitudes = [0, 30, 45, 60] colors = ['#d9534f', '#f0ad4e', '#0275d8', '#5cb85c'] fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5), dpi=150) for lat, col in zip(latitudes, colors): lam = np.radians(lat) d_east_cm = (2.0 * np.sqrt(2.0) / 3.0) * Omega * np.cos(lam) * np.sqrt(h**3 / g) * 100.0 # Convert to cm ax.plot(h, d_east_cm, '-', color=col, linewidth=2.2, label=f'Latitude $\\lambda = {lat}^\\circ$') ax.set_title('Coriolis Eastward Deflection vs. Drop Height $h$', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold', pad=10) ax.set_xlabel('Tower / Drop Height $h$ (meters)', fontsize=11) ax.set_ylabel('Eastward Deflection $d_{\\text{east}}$ (centimeters)', fontsize=11) ax.axvline(100, color='gray', linestyle=':', label='100 m Tower Benchmark') ax.legend(frameon=True, fontsize=9.5) ax.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.6) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Coriolis Eastward Deflection d_east as a function of drop height h across multiple terrestrial latitudes. Deflection scales superlinearly as h^(3/2), producing measurable centimeter-scale deviations for tall towers.](index_files/figure-html/fig-coriolis-deflection-output-1.png){#fig-coriolis-deflection width=1332 height=732} ::: ::: --- ## 7.
